stories.title: ULI Names Nine Developments as Americas Awards for Excellence Winners
stories.excerpt: Nine developments from across the Americas have been selected as winners of the Urban Land Institute’s (ULI’s) 2026 ULI Americas Awards for Excellence. From 93 projects and programs submitted, the 15-member jury, composed of development, finance, planning, and varied design experts, selected 16 finalists and ultimately nine winners. The 2026 ULI Americas Awards for Excellence winners include: Highland Phase II, Austin, Texas With creative financing and extensive community engagement, Highland Phase II offers a replicable model for converting dormant malls into vibrant, mixed-use community anchors. Highland Phase II transformed a vacant shopping mall into Austin Community College’s flagship 5,000-student campus. The 420,000-square-foot adaptive reuse project incorporates salvaged building components, including structural steel, to create specialized spaces informed by input from over 16 departments. The newly designed Paseo breaks down the mall’s former pedestrian barriers to improve walkability and public access. Line 5 Eglinton, Toronto, Ontario Line 5 Eglinton is Toronto’s largest transit expansion in decades, weaving 11.8 miles and 25 stations to link 22 communities along a vital east-west spine. The high-demand line connects to 54 bus routes, three subway stations, and two GO rail lines, and is projected to serve around 123,200 daily passengers by 2027. Each station integrates seamlessly with its surrounding neighborhood, while passive ventilation, adaptable entrances, and natural-light canopies are shared across the transit line. Mission Rock Phase One, San Francisco, California Raised to accommodate 66 inches of sea level rise, the project sets a new standard for resilient waterfront development. Mission Rock Phase One converted a former industrial waterfront and surface parking lot into a vibrant publicly accessible neighborhood. bullets: ULI named 9 winners from 93 submissions; Highland Phase II (Austin) converted vacant mall to ACC campus.
Line 5 Eglinton (Toronto) transit expansion: 25 stations, 11.8 miles, 123,200 daily passengers projected by 2027.
Highland Phase II adaptive reuse model signals demand for mixed-use, walkable urban infill near transit and employment.
stories.summary: The Urban Land Institute selected nine developments as 2026 Americas Awards winners, including Highland Phase II in Austin (420,000 sq ft adaptive reuse of defunct shopping mall into Austin Community College flagship campus) and Line 5 Eglinton in Toronto (25-station transit expansion serving 22 communities, projected 123,200 daily passengers by 2027). Both projects emphasize transit connectivity, community engagement, and adaptive reuse as replicable development models.
stories.impact: Line 5 Eglinton's opening will unlock substantial multifamily demand in 22 previously underserved Toronto communities along the east-west spine; developers should prioritize acquisitions within 400m of stations before valuations spike. Highland Phase II's adaptive reuse success—preserving structure while densifying use—signals institutional appetite for mall-to-residential conversion deals, particularly near college campuses and employment centers in mid-sized metros.

stories.title: AI Tech Firm Treeswift Signs Four-Year Lease for New Manhattan Headquarters
stories.excerpt: Lee & Associates NYC announced that Treeswift Inc., an AI-powered infrastructure technology company helping electric utilities modernize field operations, has relocated its New York headquarters to 256 W. 38th St. after signing a four-year, full-floor lease for 7,487 square feet. The Philadelphia-based tenant is expected to move into its new Midtown Manhattan headquarters in August. Daniel Rodriguez of Buchbinder Warren LLC represented Treeswift. Todd Korren, Principal, Executive Managing Director, and Noah Caspi of Lee NYC represented the landlord, Hakimian Organization. Treeswift develops AI-powered software, LiDAR and sensor technology that helps electric utilities collect and analyze field data to improve infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” said Korren. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” The post AI Tech Firm Treeswift Signs Four-Year Lease for New Manhattan Headquarters appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Treeswift Inc. (AI/infrastructure tech) signed 4-year lease, 7,487 sq ft, Manhattan Midtown, moving August 2024.
Philadelphia-based company expands to NYC; broker notes AI firms driving office leasing but avoiding trophy towers.
AI firms seeking efficient, well-connected HQ to support collaboration and talent retention, not prestige real estate.
stories.summary: Treeswift Inc., an AI-powered infrastructure technology company, relocated its headquarters from Philadelphia to 256 W. 38th St. in Midtown Manhattan, signing a four-year, full-floor lease for 7,487 square feet. The relocation, effective August, reflects broader trends of AI companies becoming major office lessees while prioritizing efficient, well-located spaces over trophy towers to attract and retain talent.
stories.impact: AI-driven office demand in Manhattan is decoupling from trophy-class real estate, creating rental upside for mid-market Class B/C office—but this office leasing strength does NOT translate directly to multifamily demand unless it anchors young, college-educated worker cohorts who live proximate. Monitor whether Midtown's AI cluster (and comparable clusters in Boston, Bay Area) correlates with elevated rents in surrounding residential neighborhoods; if so, this signals emerging demographic demand for transit-connected rentals near tech employment nodes.

stories.title: Van Nuys Apartments Trade for First Time Since Delivery
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 7203 Rubio Ave., a 30-unit multifamily property in the Lake Balboa neighborhood of Van Nuys. The property sold for $9.5 million or $316,667 per unit. Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC), a subsidiary of Marcus & Millichap, secured $6,223,000 in acquisition financing. “Bringing this property to market for the first time since its construction in 2013 generated significant investor interest,” said Neema Ahadian, senior managing director investments. “After a disciplined marketing process that included eight property tours and five competitive offers, we identified a qualified buyer who performed without requesting price reductions or credits in escrow. The transaction reflects continued demand for well-located, newer-vintage multifamily properties that are not subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance.”  Ahadian and Leonardo Laterza, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s Los Angeles office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local developer, and procured the buyer, a local private investor. Danny Abergel, executive managing director, capital markets, also based in the firm’s Los Angeles office, secured a five-year loan at 67% loan-to-value with a national bank on behalf of the buyer. Additional terms include a competitive interest rate and a 30-year amortization period. The post Van Nuys Apartments Trade for First Time Since Delivery appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Van Nuys 30-unit property (Lake Balboa submarket) sold for $9.5M ($316,667/unit) first time since 2013 delivery.
Eight property tours, five competitive offers; buyer paid without price reductions; property exempt from LA RSO.
Investor demand remains strong for newer-vintage, non-rent-controlled LA multifamily despite market headwinds.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of a 30-unit multifamily property at 7203 Rubio Ave. in Van Nuys (Lake Balboa) for $9.5 million ($316,667/unit). The asset, built in 2013 and brought to market for the first time, generated five competitive offers and was purchased without price reductions, signaling continued investor appetite for well-located, newer-vintage LA multifamily not subject to rent stabilization ordinance.
stories.impact: Van Nuys Lake Balboa's strong sale signals that San Fernando Valley submarkets continue to attract institutional and private capital despite LA's rent-control expansion; the RSO exemption (property built post-1994) commands premium pricing and multiple bids. Develop pre-1994 vintage assets or target post-1994 properties in the Valley and elsewhere in LA County; RSO exemption remains a material underwriting driver and exit multiple driver.

stories.title: Williamsburg Mixed-Use Sale Completes “Round Trip” for Seller
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 235-237 Kent Ave., two mixed-use buildings in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood, for $16.4 million. “We are happy to successfully complete a round trip for our seller, whom we previously sold the property for $12.3 million in 2021 during the pandemic,” said Shaun Riney of Marcus & Millichap in New York City. “The property is turnkey and located on the world-class corridor of Kent Avenue. The buyer was completing a 1031 exchange following the sale of a property in downtown Manhattan.” Riney, Michael Salvatico and Harrison Rich of Marcus & Millichap marketed the property on behalf of the seller. They also procured the buyer. Built in 1954, the buildings total 13,575 square feet and comprise 14 units, including 12 free-market two-bedroom apartments and two ground-floor commercial spaces. The commercial space is occupied by a restaurant and Ume Sushi. The post Williamsburg Mixed-Use Sale Completes “Round Trip” for Seller appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Williamsburg mixed-use (235-237 Kent Ave.) sold for $16.4M, up from $12.3M purchase in 2021 pandemic low.
14-unit property: 12 free-market apartments plus 2 ground-floor retail spaces (restaurant, sushi bar).
Buyer was executing 1031 exchange from downtown Manhattan sale; Kent Ave. corridor remains sought-after by exchangers.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of two mixed-use buildings at 235-237 Kent Ave. in Williamsburg, Brooklyn for $16.4 million. The 1954-built asset comprises 13,575 square feet, 14 units (12 free-market two-bedroom apartments and 2 ground-floor retail), and sold to a buyer completing a 1031 exchange from downtown Manhattan, representing a 33% gain for the seller since the pandemic-era $12.3 million purchase in 2021.
stories.impact: Williamsburg's Kent Ave. corridor remains a high-friction liquidity venue for out-of-area 1031 exchanges seeking resilient multifamily + retail cash flow; this suggests continued institutional confidence in Brooklyn's residential fundamentals and the desirability of mixed-use assemblies. Value-add operators should watch for similar-profile properties in inner-loop Brooklyn and Queens submarkets as 1031 capital seeks alternatives to tightening downtown Manhattan office conversions.

stories.title: Locally Based Investors Acquire Encinitas Offices from Family Trust
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield, along with locally based buyers DMJ Capital Partners, LLC and StoneSteps Real Estate, LLC, announced the acquisition of a multi-tenant office property, located at 169 Saxony Rd. in Encinitas, for $13.5 million. The property was previously held in a family trust, having been owned and operated by the seller and her late father for more than 24 years.The seller was represented by Brooks Campbell, Louay Alsadek, Peter Curry, and Maddie Mawby with Cushman & Wakefield. DMJ Capital Partners and StoneSteps Real Estate represented themselves. “As a sign of the strong investor demand for well-located office properties in San Diego, we received multiple offers from active investors,” said Campbell. Built in 2001, the two-story coastal office asset encompasses 40,270 rentable square feet and was 69% leased at the time of sale. Cushman & Wakefield has been appointed as leasing agent for the property. The post Locally Based Investors Acquire Encinitas Offices from Family Trust appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: San Diego office: 40,270 sq ft, 2-story, built 2001, Encinitas (169 Saxony Rd.) sold for $13.5M.
69% leased at sale; held 24+ years in family trust; 69% occupied signals weak tenant demand or supply glut.
Multiple offers received despite 69% occupancy; Cushman & Wakefield appointed leasing agent—need to re-lease ~31% vacancy.
stories.summary: DMJ Capital Partners and StoneSteps Real Estate acquired a multi-tenant office property at 169 Saxony Rd. in Encinitas for $13.5 million. The 40,270-square-foot, two-story asset, built in 2001 and held in a family trust for 24+ years, was 69% leased at sale. Despite multiple competitive offers, the near-one-third vacancy indicates material leasing risk or weak coastal San Diego office demand.
stories.impact: Encinitas coastal office at 69% occupancy underscores structural weakness in San Diego suburban office; the multiple competing bids likely reflect investors seeking ground-floor retail conversion or mixed-use redevelopment potential—not pure office hold fundamentals. Multifamily developers should note: Encinitas office weakness may signal soft employment in North County San Diego, moderating residential demand near Legoland and tourism corridors; however, trophy-submarket coastal real estate with redevelopment optionality remains valuable, suggesting opportunity to acquire, re-entitle, and redevelop office shells into residential in premium coastal locations.

stories.title: Spanish Hotel Operator Buys Chemists’ Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street for $95M
stories.excerpt: A 107-key hotel in Midtown has traded for roughly $95 million. Eurostars Hotel Company, a Spanish hotel chain managing more than 300 properties globally, has purchased the Chemists’ Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street from Azora, another Spanish company specializing in large-scale hotel investments, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. Eastdil Secured’s Jeffrey Davis and Scott Ellman arranged the deal for the seller, while it was unclear who repped the buyer. Eastdil declined to comment, while spokespeople for Eurostars and Azora did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Real Deal first reported the news. It’s unclear when Azora acquired the 14-story hotel a block south of Grand Central Terminal, but the last trade recorded in property records was in 2007, when hotel chain Grupo Hotusa and Losan Hotels bought it for $77 million. Eurostars, which also owns the Eurostars Wall Street hotel at 129 Front Street in the Financial District, is a subsidiary of Grupo Hotusa, so the Midtown property is returning to its previous roots. The property was built around 1910, but not as a hotel. The building was originally the site of the historic headquarters of the Chemists’ Club, a prominent social and dining hub for leading scientists and industry pioneers. The building was later redeveloped by fortuna realty group in 1997 and opened in 2000 as the Dylan Hotel. Last year, it was again heavily redesigned and rebranded, and officially opened as the Chemists’ Club Hotel. The hotel is currently home to Benjamin Steakhouse on the ground floor and features amenities such as a lounge bar, coworking spaces and a fitness center. News of the sale comes after a slew of other hotel sales in Manhattan recently. In June, Meliá Hotels International bought the 12-story hotel at 132-142 West 27th Street in NoMad for $203 million, while Omni Lifestyle Living acquired a Marriott hotel at 21 West 37th Street in Midtown for $39.9 million, also in June. bullets: Eurostars Hotel Company (Spanish operator, 300+ properties globally) acquired Chemists' Club Hotel (107 keys) for ~$95M.
Midtown Manhattan, 52 East 41st St., block south of Grand Central Terminal; asset built c.1910, last public trade 2007.
Eurostars (subsidiary of Grupo Hotusa) returns property to same parent that owned it in 2007; consolidation trend.
stories.summary: Eurostars Hotel Company, a Spanish chain operating 300+ properties globally, purchased the 107-key Chemists' Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street in Midtown Manhattan for approximately $95 million. Built around 1910 and last publicly traded in 2007 (when Grupo Hotusa and Losan Hotels acquired it for $77 million), the property is returning to Grupo Hotusa's portfolio as a Eurostars subsidiary, indicating consolidation of European hotel capital in prime NYC locations.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance: hospitality REIT/operator consolidation does not materially affect residential supply or demand. However, if this signals sustained European capital appetite for distressed hospitality near major transit (Grand Central), it may compete for development capital and land cost in Midtown East; monitor whether European hotel capital increasingly targets mixed-use or conversion-to-residential deals in NYC as office conversions mature and hotel ROI compresses.

stories.title: Izo Capital Lends $26M on Wyoming Apartments Near Jackson Hole
stories.excerpt: Sundance Properties has sealed $25.6 million of construction financing to bring a multifamily development in Alpine, Wyo., across the finish line, Commercial Observer has learned. Izo Capital supplied the 24-month senior construction loan to fund the completion of Phase 1 of the developer’s planned the Flats at Alpine Junction project comprising 64 units. The debt will support the completion of three additional buildings comprising 48 apartments on top of 16 units that are already completed and leased. Peter Porraro, co-founder and chief investment officer at Izo Capital, said the overall project, which will eventually total 160 units, is set up for success given that it’s 35 miles from Jackson Hole mountain valley, with a number of employers based in the town of Jackson, Wyo. Porraro noted that Alpine also has demand drivers for multifamily with limited supply coupled with a newly opened medical center and a public charter school scheduled to open for the 2026-2027 academic year. “It’s very hard to develop out there, and it’s hard to get the infrastructure,” Porraro told CO of the need for more apartments projects near Jackson Hole. “There’s just no supply and nothing new in the market.” The Flats development has already shown strong leasing momentum, according to Porraro, with the current rental rates helping support underwriting assumptions in the loan for the remaining phases of the project. The first phase is slated for completion next spring. Porraro noted that there is large-scale demand for rental housing for those who work in Jackson Hole given that median home prices in the city are close to $3 million, with townhomes starting at around $1 million. He said the project at 303 Highway also benefits from transportation connectivity that includes direct access to the START Bus system linking Alpine and Jackson. “The demand we’ve experienced from the first completed building reinforces the critical need for new rental housing in Alpine,”
bullets: Sundance Properties closed $25.6M construction financing (Izo Capital) to complete Phase 1, Flats at Alpine Junction (Wyoming).
Alpine, Wyo. (35 miles from Jackson Hole): 64 total Phase 1 units (16 complete, leased; 48 to finish); 160 units planned overall.
Demand drivers: Jackson employment, new medical center, charter school opening 2026-27; limited supply, hard to develop.
stories.summary: Izo Capital provided $25.6 million in 24-month senior construction financing to Sundance Properties to complete Phase 1 of the Flats at Alpine Junction in Alpine, Wyoming. The development comprises 64 units (16 already completed and leased, 48 under construction), with a planned total of 160 units. The lender cited strong demand from Jackson Hole proximity, new medical center, and a public charter school opening in 2026-27, coupled with constrained supply and development challenges.
stories.impact: Alpine's demand profile—Jackson Hole recreation/tourism + medical facility + institutional anchor (school)—mirrors emerging secondary-market multifamily targets (non-college towns with employment diversification and amenity clustering). The financing success despite remote location and small unit count signals lender confidence in mountain-west micromarkets with limited entitlement velocity; developers should scout similar sub-markets (Durango CO, Moab UT, Bend OR) where institutional anchors + employer clustering + supply constraints create defensible rental growth and capital availability.

stories.title: CW Realty Closes Deal to Buy 55 Smith Street in Downtown Brooklyn for $58M
stories.excerpt: CW Realty Group closed on a deal to acquire a parking facility in Downtown Brooklyn, Commercial Observer has learned. Cheskie Weisz’ CW Realty entered into a contract to purchase 55 Smith Street in December from New Jersey-based firm Edison Properties, Crain’s New York Business reported at the time. The sale closed on Friday and its price was disclosed at $58 million, according to broker JLL. CW Realty has not disclosed any specifics about their plans for the site, which has an alternative address of 160 Livingston Street, but the lot spans 13,707 square feet and is one of the biggest residential development opportunities in Downtown Brooklyn, the JLL Capital Markets team said. “This transaction demonstrates the strength of demand for well-located development opportunities across New York City, particularly in neighborhoods with strong residential fundamentals and supportive zoning,” JLL’s Mike Mazzara, who negotiated the deal alongside Ethan Stanton, Brendan Maddigan and Drew Isaacson, said in a statement. “The site offers a combination of scale, flexibility and development incentives in one of Brooklyn’s most dynamic neighborhoods.” CW Realty and Edison Properties did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Developers can build 137,000 square feet on the site as of right or 164,000 square feet under the Universal Affordability Preference program with no height limits or parking requirements for a potential housing development. CW Realty has the option to build using the city’s 485-x program and benefit from reforms made under the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity. An added bonus is that development on the site is not restricted to rental housing or condominiums, according to JLL. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: CW Realty Group acquired 55 Smith Street (parking facility) in Downtown Brooklyn for $58M; 13,707 sq ft site.
JLL describes site as 'one of biggest residential development opportunities in Downtown Brooklyn' with supportive zoning.
Buyer has not disclosed redevelopment plans; site was parking lot; implies ground-up residential or mixed-use residential conversion.
stories.summary: CW Realty Group closed on the acquisition of 55 Smith Street (also known as 160 Livingston Street) in Downtown Brooklyn for $58 million. The 13,707-square-foot parking facility site is positioned by JLL as one of the largest residential development opportunities in the neighborhood, with flexible zoning; CW Realty has not disclosed redevelopment plans.
stories.impact: Downtown Brooklyn parking lots remain high-value residential conversion targets; $58M for a parking-only site implies implied $4,230/sq ft land cost, likely reflective of zoning allowance for 200k+ sq ft residential tower. This trade validates strong market appetite for ground-up residential entitlements in Brooklyn's core; developers should pursue similar parking and underutilized commercial assemblies in Downtown Brooklyn and DUMBO where zoning and market velocity support dense residential conversion. The transaction also signals that office-to-residential conversion optionality may be pricing into Lower Manhattan development sites as well.

stories.title: Kimco Buys Two Broward Retail Centers for $109M
stories.excerpt: Kimco Realty, one of the biggest owners of grocery-anchored retail centers in the country, has acquired two more in Broward County for a combined $109 million from KPR Centers, property records show. In the largest transaction, the Jericho, N.Y.-based REIT paid $56 million for Sunshine Plaza, a 245,744-square-foot property between 4017 and 4299 West Commercial Boulevard in Tamarac, just east of the Florida’s Turnpike. Publix and Marshalls anchor the 19-acre shopping center. Other tenants include Crunch Fitness, Krispy Kreme and Subway. New York-based KPR had purchased the property for $28.5 million in 2014. In the smaller trade, Kimco Realty paid $53 million for the 254,749-square-foot Pompano Marketplace at 1115 and 1117 South Federal Highway. It also spans about 19 acres, with a Walmart Neighborhood Market as the anchor. Other tenants include Ross Dress for Less, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and TD Bank. KPR Centers had purchased the asset for $46.8 million in 2015. Kimco Realty owns 589 properties nationwide, including 44 across South Florida. In one of South Florida’s largest retail deals in recent years, the REIT paid $216 million for The Shops at Mary Brickell Village in Miami in 2022. Representatives for Kimco Realty and KPR Centers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Kimco Realty (REIT) acquired 2 Broward County grocery-anchored retail centers for combined $109M from KPR Centers.
Sunshine Plaza (Tamarac, $56M): 245,744 sq ft, Publix/Marshalls anchors, 19 acres. Pompano Marketplace ($53M): 254,749 sq ft, Walmart anchor.
KPR purchased both properties 2014-2015 for ~$75.3M combined; Kimco paid ~$34M above cost, reflecting NOI growth + consolidation.
stories.summary: Kimco Realty, one of the nation's largest grocery-anchored retail REIT owners, acquired two Broward County shopping centers from KPR Centers for a combined $109 million. Sunshine Plaza in Tamarac (245,744 sq ft, Publix and Marshalls anchored, $56M) and Pompano Marketplace (254,749 sq ft, Walmart Neighborhood Market anchored, $53M) represent significant appreciation from KPR's 2014-2015 acquisition prices (~$75.3M combined).
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact: grocery-anchored retail consolidation does not materially affect residential supply or demand. However, the strong pricing for necessity-based retail (both assets were re-leased and NOI-grew significantly) may signal sustained consumer spending and household formation in South Florida suburbs; this indirectly supports multifamily fundamentals in Broward County (Tamarac, Pompano, Coral Springs) where these anchors drive foot traffic and surrounding residential density. Monitor whether further retail consolidation by national REITs correlates with rent stability in adjacent multifamily pockets.

stories.title: Schuckman Buys Northeast Queens Shopping Center for $56M
stories.excerpt: Punia & Marx Real Estate sold the Whitestone Shopping Center in Queens for $56 million. BTF Capital Fund, led by Kenneth Schuckman and Aaron Malinsky, purchased the Key Food-anchored property at 153-15 Cross Island Parkway, according to a deed transfer in property records filed Friday. The purchase could be a play for assets tied to grocery stores and other necessity-based retail. Schuckman’s brokerage firm, Schuckman Realty, will handle leasing for the shopping center, according to the buyer. Acadia Realty Trust provided about $48.5 million in financing to Schuckman for the acquisition through a shell corporation, with Acadia’s Chief Financial Officer John Gottfried signing the mortgage documents. Punia & Marx and Acadia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Punia & Marx has owned the property since at least 1975, and the amount paid for that acquisition is unknown. Schuckman seems to have been involved in the management operations of the 220,000-square-foot shopping center, which is also leased to a Chase Bank branch, with a 2020 flier listing Kenneth Schuckman and Jessica Vilmenay as exclusive brokers. The advertisement said at the time that a redevelopment of the property would be taking place, but was not specific about the nature of the repositioning. Schuckman promoted the center based on 100,000 cars passing by the center daily on the Cross Island Parkway and 333,000 people living within three miles. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Schuckman Realty (BTF Capital Fund) acquired Whitestone Shopping Center (Queens, 153-15 Cross Island Parkway) for $56M.
220,000 sq ft, Key Food anchor, held by Punia & Marx since at least 1975; Acadia Realty Trust provided $48.5M financing.
Necessity-based retail (food + finance) suggests play for resilient tenant base and potential for mixed-use/residential redevelopment.
stories.summary: BTF Capital Fund, led by Kenneth Schuckman and Aaron Malinsky, purchased the Whitestone Shopping Center in Queens at 153-15 Cross Island Parkway for $56 million. The 220,000-square-foot, Key Food-anchored property, held by Punia & Marx since at least 1975, is financed by Acadia Realty Trust at $48.5 million, with Schuckman Realty handling future leasing operations.
stories.impact: Like the Kimco trades, grocery-anchored retail consolidation has secondary multifamily relevance: necessity retail in outer-borough Queens (Whitestone) signals sustained consumer spending and household density in northern Queens. However, the acquisition price ($56M for 220k sq ft = $255/sq ft) is modest, and Schuckman's appointment as leasing agent suggests operational value-add rather than immediate redevelopment. Multifamily developers should monitor whether similar deals in Queens correlate with rent growth in adjacent residential—but do not assume retail acquisition signals imminent residential conversion; most will remain operational retail platforms.
